title: Oeufs en Cocotte
subtitle: Baked eggs in cream with herbs
excerpt: Eggs broken into buttered ramekins with a spoonful of cream and baked in a bain-marie until the whites are just set and the yolks are still runny. One of the simplest and most elegant of French egg dishes.
sourceNotes: Oeufs en cocotte (eggs in little pots) is one of the basic preparations of the French egg repertoire. Auguste Escoffier, Le Guide Culinaire (1903), establishes several variations. Elizabeth David, French Provincial Cooking (1960), gives a plain cream version with tarragon. The bain-marie method is essential: it allows the eggs to cook in very gentle heat so the whites set without the yolks firming.

glossaryTerms.definition: A water bath. Ramekins or other containers are placed inside a larger dish filled with hot water and the whole assembly goes into the oven. The water surrounds the smaller containers with gentle, even heat, preventing the contents from over-cooking or curdling. Used for custards, delicate egg dishes, and terrines.

content.text: Oeufs en cocotte are eggs baked in small ramekins with cream, in a

. The water bath keeps the heat gentle enough to set the whites without hardening the yolks. The result, when the timing is right, is a white that is just trembling and a yolk that runs when the surface is broken with a spoon. Serve with good bread and unsalted butter.
The cream version here is the simplest. Variations include a spoonful of mushroom duxelles in the base, a few lardons, or smoked salmon, all go in before the egg.
Heat the oven to 180°C fan. Boil a full kettle of water. Butter the ramekins generously. Place a tarragon leaf in the base of each if using.
Pour 1 tbsp of cream into each ramekin. Season with salt and a little white pepper. Break one egg into each ramekin, keeping the yolk intact.
Place the ramekins in the roasting tin. Pour boiling water into the tin until it comes halfway up the sides of the ramekins. Place in the oven.

Bake for 10 to 12 minutes. The whites should be just set, opaque but still trembling slightly, and the yolks runny. Begin checking at 10 minutes; the eggs will continue to cook from the residual heat of the ramekin after they come out of the oven.
Remove from the water bath, scatter with chives, and serve immediately with bread for dipping.

items.cause: The eggs cooked for too long, or the oven was too hot.
items.fix: Reduce the cooking time next time. The eggs should come out of the oven while the whites still appear slightly underdone, carry-over cooking in the hot ramekin will finish them.

items.symptom: The whites are still liquid after 12 minutes
items.cause: The water in the bain-marie was cold rather than boiling, or the oven temperature was too low.
items.fix: The water must be boiling when it goes into the tin. Cold water needs 10 to 15 minutes to come to temperature and means the eggs will not cook in the expected time.

items.cause: The temperature of the bain-marie was too high, the water was boiling vigorously.
items.fix: Keep the oven at 180°C maximum. The water in the bain-marie should steam but not boil vigorously. If it boils, the cream curdles and the eggs cook unevenly.

content.text: The cocotte, a small earthenware or porcelain pot, is one of the most useful vessels in the French kitchen. It serves for everything from individual terrines to braised vegetables. Oeufs en cocotte are one of its most classic uses, appearing in the egg chapter of French cookery books from Escoffier onwards. They are also one of the most adaptable: the base can be varied with almost anything to hand, and the cooking time is never more than 12 minutes.
